text: hey everybody the Bible contradicts itself in many different places and in many different ways and that's just not really up for serious debate but that
does not mean that every proposed contradiction has to be accepted as a contradiction there are many different cases where a better translation or
manuscript or a better reconstruction of the historical context or of the literary conventions can help us resolve
two passages that might at first appear to conflict with each other and sometimes Scholars will tentatively and
responsibly propose hypothetical scenarios that reconcile two passages
provided those hypothetical scenarios constitute more plausible explanations for how the passages got to be the way
they are then explanations that just acknowledge that they conflict with each other now this is different from the
apologetic approach of denying that there are any contradictions in the Bible and there are a handful of methodological problems with this
approach one of the most foundational is the insistence on a very specific and a
very narrow and Technical definition of the word contradiction and this definition insists that contradictions
only exist if there is no possible way that two different propositions can be true at the same time and if we accept
that definition then as long as I can imagine any possible scenario or combination of
scenarios that reconcile these two propositions there is no contradiction and that lowers the bar literally to the
ground because as long as there's no limit to the number of scenarios you can imagine you can reconcile any two
passages or any two propositions and this lowering of the bar to the ground is intentional because it makes the
threshold possibility meaning it is only a contradiction if it is totally
impossible to reconcile it and since it's not really totally impossible to reconcile anything you can always gin up that tiniest little sliver of not
impossible now this highlights that the target audience for these arguments is not Scholars because Scholars are not
looking for the tiniest little sliver of not impossible they're looking for what's plausible what's probable and this does not remotely meet those
evidentiary standards even though it has to perform as if it is for critical scholarship the target audience is
people who already believe and just want to feel justified in that belief and for most of them they are just looking for
that tiny little sliver of not impossible and that is what apologetics delivers
